description: Just For Fun: a one-person crew from Ukraine working on the astronaut health monitoring challenge. Ideas come from the human; Super Intelligence tools help with code and research, and every SI-assisted part will be disclosed per Space Apps rules. The crew is complete, so we are not recruiting.
summary: On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting changes in their own health, often with no doctor on board and a slow or broken link to Earth. Crew Health Console is a working prototype that gathers a crew member's health readings in one program that runs offline. Plain automation, with no AI needed, compares each number with its norm and with red limits from published sources (drafts): a dangerous value raises an alert at once, while changes common in flight stay quiet. Each crew member sees one dated sentence about body and mind, the reasons and, when something is off, a choice: Details, Analyse with AI, or Message the doctor. Version 1.4.0 adds a small open AI model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, WebLLM) that runs on the computer itself, only after the person agrees, and nothing written leaves the computer. It follows written rules, each with its source: risk words open Help now first, code checks every answer (no diagnoses, no medicines, no overruling the automation), and rules for space: it knows how far Earth is, never promises a quick reply on Mars, and points first to the crew medical officer on board. Without a suitable graphics chip, everything else keeps working. A 3-minute Earth break shows real video and sound of rain, fields, a city, a cafe, the sea and a forest. Real data from NASA's Open Science Data Repository are inside: the Inspiration4 crew's blood tests. Display and alert rules are modelled on NASA-STD-3001. Not a medical device.
details:
Live: https://neveleren.github.io/space-apps-2026-crew-health/
Code: https://github.com/neveleren/space-apps-2026-crew-health
The public copy runs without the program's own server, so what a visitor enters stays in their own browser. The full version with the server runs on one computer with npm start (see the README).

The idea (the human member's)

  • Everything needed to watch a crew's health already exists in pieces: sensors, smart clothing, wearables, lab analyzers, automation and AI. The idea is to connect them into one machine: plain automation as the base, the AI and people on top. The model is aviation automation such as Garmin Autoland, which can land a plane by itself in an emergency such as pilot incapacitation.
  • Who notices a problem depends on who is there: the astronaut alone, a crewmate, the AI, or a doctor on Earth. So the program must keep working when the AI or the link fails.
  • Numbers go to simple cells: heart rate is compared with its norm. Complex data, such as an X-ray, go to the AI or a doctor.
  • Four norms per measure: general on Earth, general in space, personal on Earth, personal in space.
  • A back side that holds every factor in order, and a front side that tells the person only what is really wrong, in plain words, with a choice.
  • The mind matters as much as the body: daily check-ins, then an anonymous talk with AI support or the results to the doctor, as the person chooses. And a private cycle tracker, "like Flo, but for astronauts".
  • The effort of a measurement on the team's scale: light (pulse, blood pressure, sugar, breathing, radiation), high (CT, ECG, ultrasound), extreme (blood).

What it does
Today: one sentence, a reason, a choice. Each crew member signs in and sees a dated sentence, for example "As of 15 Nov 2026, your physical condition needs attention, your mental condition is excellent.", then the reasons and, when the body needs attention, the buttons Details, Analyse with AI and Message the doctor. For the mind, AI support offers, in the team's own words, an anonymous talk or to send the check-ins to the doctor; the person chooses. The levels use the display colours of NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2 (attention blue, needs action yellow, urgent red, stale data cyan), always with an icon and a word as well. Mapping health levels to NASA's alert classes is the team's design and needs the flight surgeons' approval.

It speaks up only when something is really wrong (all thresholds are drafts):

  • One reading past a red limit counts at once, for example a resting heart rate of 131 or more (NEWS2), glucose below 54 mg/dL (ADA) or a cabin pressure below 34.5 kPa (NASA-STD-3001).
  • A daily vital sign just outside its norm needs 3 readings in a row, unless two or more vital signs are out within 24 hours (the reasoning of NEWS2).
  • Changes common in flight are information, not alarms: resting body temperature up to about 1 °C higher (Stahn et al., 2017; 38.0 °C or more always counts as a fever, CDC) and sleep of 5 hours or more (ISS crews slept about 6 hours a night, Barger et al., 2014). A heart rate taken during exercise is recorded, not judged.
  • With no fresh data, the sentence says so and never says "excellent".

Urgent help needs no AI and no link. A reading past an urgent limit, the camera alarm or the Help key (hold it for 2 seconds) sounds the alarm, repeated until someone acknowledges it. Within seconds every crew screen in use shows one line, for example "Tom needs help now: Blood oxygen (SpO2) 85 %.", and nothing else of the record (the ISS crew code of conduct, 14 CFR 1214.403). The program also writes the message to the doctor by itself: to the doctor on board, or sealed in the outbox for Earth, where it waits while there is no link. "I am okay: false alarm" clears the line on every screen. In this prototype the doctor and the link are simulated by switches.

38 measures in the machine: vital signs, glucose, sleep, fluids, body mass, the eyes (pressure, OCT, an Amsler grid self-check), hearing, radiation dose, fitness and strength, bone, blood tests, X-ray, ECG, ultrasound, symptoms, medicines, exercise, the camera, the mind (mood, energy, sleep quality, a thinking test, a reaction test, the topics that weigh on the person), the menstrual cycle, and the cabin air (CO2, oxygen, pressure, temperature, noise). On the crew screen they sit in fixed groups and can be found by everyday words ("sugar" finds glucose). Numbers and self-reports such as mood or the eye self-check have a page each: the level, a table of readings and, for numbers, a chart (7 days, 30 days, the whole flight, before flight, all, or custom dates) with the normal band and any red limit lines, the four norms with their sources and, for most, "Log a reading by hand". A forecast line to landing, labelled "not a medical model", is drawn only for slow changes (fitness, strength, body mass, radiation, hearing) or a clear trend. "What to do" steps come with each alert. Images and tracings say that they go to the AI or a doctor; the cycle, symptoms and medicines have private cards.

One medical record, everything in one place. The answer to NASA's own words above: a fifth key opens everything the program holds about the astronaut, read only, like the patient's card of Ukraine's e-health system: measures, lab results, eye checks and images, medicines and symptoms, every alert and what happened to it, messages to the doctor, and the private mind and cycle sections. What a prototype cannot hold (allergies, vaccinations, diagnoses) is listed with the reason.

Before critical work and before landing. In the 24 hours before a spacewalk, a docking or robotic arm work, a readiness card puts together last night's sleep, sleep and sedating medicines and the reaction test. From 30 days before landing, aerobic capacity and strength against NASA's 80% of pre-flight, recent exercise and the last eye exam; after landing, a recovery phase. All windows are drafts with their sources.

Private logs that help the doctor. A month calendar for the menstrual cycle (bleeding and symptoms, breakthrough bleeding while suppressed, no fertility features), and a weekly doctor summary that holds symptoms, medicines with the kit list's own warnings, exercise, reaction tests and the eyes, only if the astronaut sends it.

Ready for an analog test such as HERA. Every alert is logged with its time to acknowledge, a second screen agrees on what was read, drills sound like real alarms but never count, and a de-identified study export is built in.

Real NASA data. Sign in as one of the four Inspiration4 participants (C001 to C004) to see their real blood tests from NASA OSDR: seven blood draws, from 92 days before launch to 194 days after return, each against the lab's own range. They are never mixed with the made-up crew.

Daily use. A short check-in (mood, energy, sleep quality, and optional private topics), quick logs for symptoms and medicines, and "Coming up", an example schedule after NASA's routine: the weekly private medical conference with a one-page summary to prepare it, the private talk with the psychologist every two weeks, the monthly thinking test and the eye checks.

Mind support that works with no AI and no link (added at the human member's request, from NASA studies and other published research; docs/MIND_SUPPORT.md): small things that help, each with its source; a private journal; my plan for hard days, with "Talk to a person now"; problem solving in five steps; a 3-minute Earth break with real video of six places on Earth (rain on a forest trail, a wheat field, a city, a cafe, the sea, a forest), each with its own recorded sound: a mix moves through the scenes by default, with a scene chooser, mute and volume, and a still frame when the device asks for reduced motion; the files are in the program, so it works offline (videos from Pexels, sounds from Freesound under CC0, credited on screen and in assets/breathe/CREDITS.md); a 3-minute reaction test modelled on NASA's Reaction Self Test. The anonymous AI session opens with a privacy card ("This is AI support: a program, not a person and not a psychologist.") and has a "Help now" card with fixed steps to reach a person. Since 1.4.0 the session holds a real chat with the local AI (below); Help now and the coping steps still work with the AI off.

A local AI with rules (new in 1.4.0). "Analyse with AI" and the anonymous session now run a real AI model on the computer: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Apache-2.0) in a 4-bit build, with the WebLLM 0.2.87 engine (Apache-2.0) bundled in the program. It starts only after the person agrees on a card that says what downloads, how big (about 880 MB), from where, and that it runs on this computer and nothing written leaves it. On board, the model comes from the program's own folder, filled once with node tools/fetch-model.mjs, so nothing downloads in flight. The public demo downloads it once from Hugging Face, fixed to one revision, with the configuration, tokenizer and GPU program checked by SHA-256; then the browser keeps it and it starts with no network. It needs WebGPU with 16-bit float shaders and about 1.6 GB of graphics memory. Measured on the team's laptop (NVIDIA RTX 3050 Ti, Edge): ready in 4.5 to 7.1 s from the on-board folder, the first answer in 24 to 38 s (this includes compiling the programs for the graphics chip), later answers in 0.8 to 16 s. On laptops with two graphics chips the browser must use the high-performance one, and the panel says so.
It follows 27 rules in one file (src/ai-rules.js), each with its source, in three layers. Before the model: risk words open Help now first and that message never reaches the model; the private logs never go in. In the prompt: the rules as plain sentences, with the automation's level and the flagged readings with their norms and sources. After the model: code checks every answer before it is shown and holds diagnoses, medicine names and doses, claims to be a person or a doctor, advice that ignores or contradicts the automation's levels and alarms, and putting off action when a reading is red. A held answer is replaced by a fixed text that names the rule; only a count is kept, never the text. Both panels show "Rules this AI follows", and the explanation is marked "AI draft, not a diagnosis". How it works in space (rules approved by the human member on 15 Nov 2026, shown in both panels with their NASA sources): it knows where the crew is (ISS, Moon or Mars) and never promises a quick answer from Earth on Mars, where a reply takes at least twice a one-way delay of up to about 22 minutes (NASA HRP-48021); with no link to Earth it says a message to the doctor waits in the outbox and never says to contact Earth now; when Earth is far it points first to the crew medical officer and crewmates on board (NASA-STD-3001 [V1 3004], [V1 3006]); it speaks of itself only as a program, never claiming feelings (Volume 2, Appendix F.6.2); and its mode shows in the status line, with a notice when it changes ([V2 10161], [V2 10162]). With no WebGPU, no usable graphics chip, a failed download, a chip that drops the model, or the "AI is working" switch off, the panels run in rules-only mode and everything else works as before. The AI never sends a message or calls anyone, and the levels and red limits stay the automation's alone. Its limits: a 1.5B model does not always follow its prompt (it does not always end by pointing to a person), so the hard rules are the code checks before and after the model; seven rules are marked TO CONFIRM for the team.

Camera (optional; Google MediaPipe models run on the computer). A hand held to the chest first asks "Are you okay?" on screen and aloud; only "I need help" or no answer within 20 seconds raises the alarm. A sleeping person is ignored, feelings are never read from the face or the voice, the camera turns itself off after an hour, and video is never stored or sent. A demonstration, not a medical device.

Around the screen. Alarm tones after NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2, Table 10.3-1, the first one 10 dB quieter, with a sound test. A status line that is always there: flight day, GMT clock, system state, Messages and Help. Messages say honestly where a letter to the doctor is: sealed in the outbox, waiting for the link, or saved on this computer only. Settings: display, mission profile (ISS, Moon or Mars), Connections, a copy of my data, an optional PIN and simulation switches. A technical view (machine.html) shows where each reading went and why.

How it works

  • Automation first, AI second, doctor when needed (the team's logic). Every reading is an event that goes to its own cell; a number is compared with its norm. Inside the norm, nothing more happens. Outside it, the reading is handed to the AI step (in the machine still simulated; the local AI explains readings when the person asks) or, with the AI off, marked as not decided yet; the levels on the screen come from plain rules either way. Past a red limit, the automation alone, with no AI, alerts the person and routes the case to the crew on board and to a doctor (the doctor and the link are simulated here); an urgent case reaches every crewmate's screen at once. Images and tracings go to the AI or a doctor.
  • Event sourcing. On start, the machine replays all events in time order, so the history and the journal come back exactly after a restart.
  • Small and offline. HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step and no packages. A Node.js server (version 18 or newer, no dependencies) keeps one plain file per person, named by id with no personal information. Fonts, icons, the camera models, the AI engine and the Earth break videos and sounds are in the folder. On board, the AI model's files (876 MB) are put into the program's folder once, with node tools/fetch-model.mjs, so the program needs no internet. Only the two live Earth demos, off by default, use it, and on the public site the one-time model download from Hugging Face, after the person agrees.
  • Privacy and security, as a demonstration (docs/SECURITY.md). The crew screen loads only the signed-in person's records, the cabin readings and crewmates' alarm lines. An optional PIN keeps only a salted PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 hash (600,000 iterations) in the browser: a privacy screen, not a lock. The server answers only known host names, accepts only JSON from its own pages, checks every event, never serves private folders, and sends security headers with a Content Security Policy. That policy allows no model host, so an on-board copy never downloads a model; only the public copy's own page allows Hugging Face. Each message to a doctor is sealed for the flight surgeon's public key (ECDH P-256, HKDF-SHA-256, AES-256-GCM) in an outbox, the hand-over point for a downlink. Not protected yet: the demo key pair is public, the server has no sign-in or roles, files at rest are plain text, messages carry no sender signature, and the downlink itself is not built.
  • Supply chain. SBOM.json (CycloneDX 1.6) names the third-party code, models and fonts with their licences and hashes, now also the WebLLM engine and the model's GPU program; SHA256SUMS gives the SHA-256 of every file in vendor/ and fonts/; the tests check both. The Earth break videos and sounds are listed with their authors and licences in assets/breathe/CREDITS.md.
  • Tested. 467 automatic tests (npm test, Node's built-in test runner) cover the machine, the levels, the forecast, the camera rules, the mind tools and the Earth break, the logs, the connections, the server's security, the PIN, the crew alarm, the supply chain and the AI's rules (what the model gets, risk words that never reach it, answers that must be held and answers that must pass). Browser scripts also walked through the main flows in a headless browser, the core ones at desktop and phone widths, and the AI ran in Edge with WebGPU on the team's laptop (those scripts are not in the repository).

Connections, each shown in Settings as Working, Simulated or Planned (docs/INTEGRATIONS.md). No NASA operational system is connected; ISSLive is NASA's public feed, used as an Earth demo.

Working:

  • Bluetooth heart rate strap, thermometer, blood pressure cuff and pulse oximeter (standard Bluetooth health profiles, unit-tested with the specifications' byte formats and examples, not yet with a physical device).
  • An HL7 FHIR R4 export with LOINC codes, UCUM units, Device, Provenance, and a "test data" label (HTEST) on made-up data; a generated file passed the official R4 JSON schema.
  • NASA OSDR Inspiration4 blood tests (a saved copy, offline).
  • Live ISS cabin air from NASA ISSLive and space weather from NOAA (Earth demos, off by default).
  • CSV import of Hexoskin, Astroskin, Philips Actiware and Svantek exports or any table (tried only with small files written from the makers' documents; the Svantek layout is guessed).
  • A calendar file (iCalendar, RFC 5545).

Simulated:

  • The link to Earth (store and forward inside the program).
  • The other devices on the technical view.

Planned (each needs NASA or a partner):

  • The station server and downlink.
  • NASA's delay-tolerant networking (HDTN).
  • EveryWear.
  • NASA's crew medical record (Chiron, ExMC Medical Data Architecture).
  • The live crew plan.
  • ISS FIT.
  • The Crew Active Dosimeter.
  • Blood analyzers on board.
  • Medical images (DICOM).
  • Watch data from before flight.
  • NASA's astronaut archives (LSDA, LSAH).

Why it matters

  • On the way to Mars, NASA's Human Research Program expects "a communication delay of up to 20 minutes one way" and says astronauts "must be capable of confronting an array of situations with minimal support from teams on Earth".
  • NASA's own crew health data project lists the problems of today's ISS health exam: "manual data collection and transfer via multiple systems", "no notifications provided", "data occasionally missing/delayed" (CHP-IDSP, HRP Investigators' Workshop 2025). This program puts the readings in one place, tells the crew member directly, and marks data that are late or missing.
  • In January 2026, a medical event on the ISS first needed immediate help from crewmates, guided by NASA flight surgeons; NASA then chose an early return for Crew-11 to use medical imaging not available on the station (NASA, 25 Feb 2026). Far from Earth, crewmates are the first help, which is why the urgent path here needs no AI and no link.

Benefits

  • Less alarm fatigue. In hospitals an estimated 85 to 99% of alarm signals need no clinical intervention (The Joint Commission, 2013). Here a single odd reading waits for a repeat, red limits still count at once, and every alert says why.
  • Help before the doctor. The person sees a change early, with the norm, the trend and the source, and chooses what to do.
  • Keeps working when the AI, the doctor or the link to Earth is missing.
  • Trust. Each norm in use and each red limit names its source, drafts are marked as drafts, and made-up data are marked as made up.
  • Privacy. Each person's records are kept apart, the journal and the plan stay in the person's browser, talks with the AI never leave the computer and are forgotten when the panel closes, and crewmates see only "needs help now".
  • For flight surgeons. One record per person, a FHIR file with LOINC codes, and sealed messages.

What we hope to achieve

  • The human member's goal: a working product that could be used in real work, by NASA or a partner agency; not a mock-up, and not made for the prizes.
  • Next steps:
  • settle the team's open decisions (below);
  • test with people: NASA-STD-3001 asks crew interfaces for an average score of 85 or more on the NASA Modified System Usability Scale [V2 10001] and Bedford workload ratings of 3 or less for nominal tasks [V2 5007]; neither is measured yet;
  • an analog mission test with flight surgeons, for example in NASA's HERA, where crews work with communication delays of up to five minutes each way: count false alarms and crew minutes per day;
  • the team's decisions on the AI marked TO CONFIRM (which model flies, the risk word list, other languages);
  • more real devices, and the planned connections with NASA and partners.
  • Readiness today: software TRL 3 to 4 by our own reading of NASA's definitions (NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E): an integrated prototype run on made-up and public data, not yet tested in a relevant environment.

Still open: the team's decisions
These stay with the human member. In the app, thresholds and limits are marked as drafts, and the technical view lists the team's main open questions.
- Which questionnaire for the mind (PHQ-9, PHQ-8, GAD-7 or another); none is built in.
- Whether to use a NEWS2 total score; today only its single red values are used, as drafts.
- The crisis rule: what happens in immediate danger during the anonymous session. Today nothing is sent by itself.
- The AI's name, and whether to call the session "anonymous" or "private".
- Which AI model flies, and whether the AI may talk in other languages (today English only).
- All level thresholds, including the mind rule (low mood or energy on 6 of the last 14 days for attention, 8 for needs action) and the rule to wait for 3 out-of-range readings in a row.
- Names for crew members 3 and 4.
- Who gives advice: the automation or the AI.
- How the program tells people apart; today each person chooses themselves.
- Whether the steps before "Message the doctor" are anonymous.
- Who analyses X-rays.
- The default when there is no doctor on board and no link (today's draft: alert the crew on board and queue the message).
- Whether to convert the ISS cabin oxygen reading to the inspired value; today it is shown, not saved.
- An upper heart-rate limit during exercise.
- Whether a resting pulse of 40 should count as urgent for athletes.
- How long a red reading of a rarely taken measure stays on the screen.
- An ISS-specific cabin pressure limit.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS; Python 3 for one build tool (tools/build_inspiration4.py).
  • Runtime: Node.js 18 or newer, built-in modules only; any modern browser. Bluetooth needs a browser with Web Bluetooth, such as Chrome or Edge (not Firefox or Safari). The AI needs a browser with WebGPU and 16-bit float shaders (shader-f16) and about 1.6 GB of graphics memory; it was tested in Edge. Without them, the AI panels run in rules-only mode.
  • Browser features: Web Bluetooth, Web Audio, Web Crypto, WebGPU (the AI), speech synthesis, the camera, video and audio playback, and SVG charts drawn by the program itself.
  • Third-party files in the repository: Google MediaPipe Tasks Vision 1.1.1 with the pose landmarker (lite) and face landmarker models (Apache-2.0); the Atkinson Hyperlegible Next and Mono 2.001 fonts by the Braille Institute (SIL Open Font License 1.1); Lucide icons from lucide-static 1.66.0 (ISC License; the icons derived from Feather are under the MIT License); the WebLLM 0.2.87 engine (Apache-2.0) with the model's compiled GPU program from the MLC project (that repository has no licence file; to confirm); six videos from Pexels (Pexels License) and six sound recordings from Freesound (CC0 1.0). The AI model, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Apache-2.0) in MLC's 4-bit build, is not in the repository: it goes into the program's folder on board or the browser's storage on the public site.
  • Standards: HL7 FHIR R4, LOINC, UCUM, the Bluetooth GATT health profiles, iCalendar (RFC 5545), CycloneDX 1.6.
  • Hardware: any computer with a modern browser; an optional webcam; optional standard Bluetooth health devices; for the AI, a graphics chip that WebGPU can use (measured on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Ti laptop chip).
  • Made and checked with: Claude (Anthropic) as the SI tool (see "Use of SI"); Git, GitHub and GitHub Pages; Playwright with headless Chromium (browser checks, screenshots and the recorded demo walks) and with Microsoft Edge on the laptop's graphics chip (the AI checks); Chromium also printed the slides PDF; FFmpeg (the demo video); ajv with the HL7 FHIR R4 JSON schema; axe-core (an accessibility check).

How SI was used (short)
The idea, the structure and every decision are the human member's. The code, the fact research, the made-up example data, the drafts of thresholds and the texts were made with SI (Claude, Anthropic). The app's code files, the page metadata, the sign-in page, Settings, every slide and the video's mark say so. The product itself also runs machine learning on the computer: Google's MediaPipe models for the camera and, since 1.4.0, an open language model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) under written rules.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Who did what. The idea, the structure, the logic and every decision come from the human member of team Just For Fun. His own sketch of 14 Nov 2026 (16:35) and his messages are kept, with times, in the team's notes. SI did not come up with the idea: when the human member asked how SI would visualise it, SI declined, because that is the core of the idea, and gave only facts.

Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, was used as a tool for:
1. Code. All of the team's own code, tests and tools in the repository were generated by SI from the team's description and decisions. The third-party files in vendor/ and fonts/ were not; they are listed under References. The app's code files say so in their header comments, and so do package.json, the README, the page metadata, the sign-in page and the About card in Settings.
2. Facts. Looking up norms, NASA practice and standards in public sources, each with its link. The facts gathered for the brainstorm were each checked by a second, adversarial SI agent that reopened the source.
3. Example data. SI chose the four made-up crew members and their example flight. They are marked as made up on every screen and in the data, and the FHIR export labels them as test data (HTEST).
4. Drafts inside the team's structure, at the human member's request: the levels and their thresholds, the variants of the dated sentence, the red limits from cited sources, the camera's 20-second wait, the extra mind-support tools built from NASA studies, the safety and privacy features modelled on NASA's requirements, the AI's rules (src/ai-rules.js, drafted from the team's own texts; seven are marked TO CONFIRM) and the choice of the Earth break videos and sounds. The page marks them as drafts for the team and the flight surgeons to decide.
5. Reviews. SI agents played a flight surgeon, a psychologist, an astronaut, NASA engineers and a judge to review the prototype. These were simulated reviews: no NASA staff member or outside expert has reviewed the project.
6. Words. Translating the human member's Russian into English, and drafting the docs, the texts of the slides and the video, and this page.

Inside the product. The product has SI/ML built in, and all of it runs on the computer. The camera demonstration runs Google's MediaPipe pose and face landmark models (machine learning). Since version 1.4.0, "Analyse with AI" and "Start an anonymous session with AI" run an open language model, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Alibaba Cloud's Qwen team, Apache-2.0; a 4-bit build by the MLC project), with the WebLLM engine, only after the person agrees. We did not train or change the model. It works under 27 written rules, each with its source, and code checks every answer before it is shown; the rules were drafted with SI (Claude) from the team's own texts, and seven are marked TO CONFIRM for the human member. Without a suitable graphics chip the AI panels say so and run in rules-only mode. This is in addition to the code made with Claude (Anthropic), disclosed above.

Images, video and audio. No SI image, video, sound or voice generator was used. The 3-minute Earth break shows real footage and plays real recordings: six videos from Pexels (Pexels License) and six sound recordings from Freesound (CC0), credited on screen and in assets/breathe/CREDITS.md. Claude chose them and cut, looped, cropped, scaled, levelled and encoded them at the human member's request; nothing in them was generated. The other pictures are Lucide icons and drawings made by the program's code (charts, the Amsler grid). The demo video and the slides show screen captures of the app and text; every video frame that shows a picture carries a visible "Made with SI (Claude)" mark, and every slide carries the line "Slides drafted with SI (Claude)". The spoken prompts ("Are you okay?", "Warning") use the browser's own speech synthesis while the app runs; the only audio files shipped are the six Earth break recordings.

No NASA branding. Nothing made with SI uses NASA logos, insignia or other NASA branding. NASA is a source of standards and data here; nothing in this project is endorsed by NASA.
